title: UK Ltd Company for Amazon Sellers: What It Is and When It Helps
headline: UK Ltd Company for Amazon Sellers: What It Is and When It Helps
description: A plain-language guide to UK limited companies for Amazon sellers: what a Ltd is, what it can and cannot do, ongoing duties and when forming one makes sense. General information only.
body_html:
Many new Amazon sellers start as individuals. Later, they hear that a limited company can help. This guide explains in plain language what a UK limited company (Ltd) is, what it can and cannot do for an Amazon seller, and what to think about before you form one. It is general information, not legal or tax advice.

What is a UK Ltd company?

A private limited company is a separate legal entity registered with Companies House, the UK company registry. The company, not you personally, owns its assets, signs contracts and holds its bank account. The owners are called shareholders and the people who run it are called directors. In many cases one person can be both.

A company must have a registered office address in the UK, at least one director, and a company name that is not already taken or too similar to another. Once registered it receives a company number that you can look up publicly.

Why some Amazon sellers use one

  • Business identity. When you open a seller account as a business, Amazon asks for business details and documents. A registered company gives you a clear legal name and number to use. See our guide on how to open an Amazon seller account.
  • Separation. Business money and contracts sit in the company rather than in your personal name. A company can also reduce personal liability in some situations, but it does not remove all responsibility, so ask a qualified adviser about your case.
  • Brand and trade mark ownership. Some sellers prefer the brand and any trade mark to belong to the company, which makes it easier to hand over or grow the business later.
  • Banking and payments. Many business bank and payment accounts are easier to open for a registered company, although each provider has its own checks.
  • Selling in the UK and Europe. If you plan to sell on the UK marketplace, having a UK company can fit neatly with your setup. It is not a requirement for every seller.

What a UK Ltd does not do

  • It does not make your Amazon account safer or give you better rankings or sales.
  • It does not remove tax duties. A company has to keep records and report to the authorities, and VAT is a separate registration with its own rules.
  • It is not required to start selling on Amazon. Many sellers begin as individuals and form a company later.
  • It does not replace good account practices. You still need accurate listings, healthy metrics and policy-compliant behaviour.

What you have to keep doing after you form it

A company is not a one-off purchase. In general, UK companies must file a yearly confirmation statement and annual accounts with Companies House, keep their records up to date, and deal with company tax. The exact deadlines and amounts depend on your situation, so check the current rules on the official UK government website or ask an accountant. We do not give tax advice.

Who owns it, and where do you live?

People who live outside the UK can often own and direct a UK company, but they still need to meet the identity checks and provide a UK registered office address. Rules around identity verification have been changing, so check the current requirements before you apply.

When does it make sense?

A company is worth considering when you are serious about running a long-term business, want the brand held by a legal entity, plan to sell in the UK, or need a business structure for banking and agreements. If you are still testing a first product, you can wait. Talk to an accountant about tax, and compare the yearly costs with what you expect to earn.

A simple checklist before you decide

  • Which Amazon marketplaces will you sell on?
  • Who will be the director and shareholder?
  • Do you have an address that can serve as the registered office?
  • Who will handle accounts, filings and tax each year?
  • Will your bank and payment providers accept the company?

If you sell across the Gulf, our guide on selling on Amazon in Saudi Arabia and the UAE explains how those marketplaces differ.
